site_article.headline: Udio vs Suno: which AI music maker to use in 2026, and the download catch
site_article.dek: Both still turn a text prompt into a song. Only Suno lets you download what you make, and even there the free plan gets almost nothing.
site_article.summary: Suno runs its v6 models and lets paid users download a set number of songs each month with commercial rights. Udio still creates and extends songs but has disabled all downloads since its Universal Music partnership in October 2025.
site_article.seo_title: Udio vs Suno: which AI music maker to use in 2026
site_article.seo_description: Udio vs Suno compared: free credits, plan prices, download limits, commercial rights and the steps to make a song in each, plus which one to pick for what.
site_article.answer_summary: Pick Suno if you need to download and use your songs: Pro and Premier include downloads and commercial use. Pick Udio only if you want to experiment and share by link, because Udio has disabled downloads since October 2025.
site_article.hero_alt: Suno's promotional graphic for its v6 music models.

paragraphs.text: Udio vs Suno used to be a question about sound quality. In late 2026 it is mostly a question about downloads. Suno launched its v6 models on September 9, 2026, and lets paying users download a set number of songs each month. Udio still makes songs, but it turned off downloads on October 29, 2025, as part of its partnership with Universal Music Group, and its help center says downloading of audio, video and stems is disabled.
Udio vs Suno at a glance

Suno: three models (v6, v6-wild and v6-mini), a free plan with 50 credits a day on v6-mini, and paid plans that add downloads, commercial rights and editing tools. Suno says v6 and v6-wild are for Pro and Premier subscribers, while v6-mini is available to everyone. The models were built in partnership with Warner Music Group, BMG and Believe, according to The Next Web.

Udio: create, extend and remix still work, including the v1, v1.5 and v1.5 Allegro models and the Styles feature, according to Udio's help page on its Warner Music deal. Songs can be shared by link. A new licensed platform has been announced but has no launch date.
Free plans and prices

Suno's free plan gives 50 credits a day and uses v6-mini, with no downloads included and no commercial rights. Suno's help center says free users who joined on or after September 3, 2026, may occasionally receive a small number of trial downloads for personal, non commercial use. Pro is listed at $10 a month and Premier at $30 a month, with discounted prices shown on the pricing page when NeuraFeed checked on November 27, 2026. Pro includes 2,500 credits and 20 downloads a month, and Premier includes 10,000 credits, 60 downloads and Suno Studio. A Platinum plan adds more credits and 120 downloads.

Suno's help center says the free plan is for non commercial use and that Pro and Premier include commercial use. Unused downloads do not roll over to the next month, extra downloads can be bought, and downloading the same song in several formats counts as one download.

Udio's free plan gives 10 credits a day plus a monthly pool of 100 credits, and its help center caps free users at three 130 second songs a day. Every create, extend, remix, inpaint or edit makes two songs and costs 2 credits for 32 second clips or 4 credits for 130 second clips. After the Universal Music deal, Udio raised paid credit limits to 2,400 for Standard and 6,000 for Pro and added a one time grant of 1,000 credits that do not expire.
How to make a song in Suno

paragraphs.title: 1. Pick Simple or Custom
paragraphs.text: In Simple Mode you describe the song in one line and Suno writes the lyrics. In Custom Mode you paste your own lyrics, fill in Style of Music and give the song a title. Turn on Instrumental if you want no vocals.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: a Simple Mode description
paragraphs.text: An upbeat indie pop song about moving to a new city in winter, female vocals, bright guitars, catchy chorus

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: a Style of Music line for Custom Mode
paragraphs.text: lo-fi hip hop, mellow piano, vinyl crackle, slow tempo, [mood: rainy evening]

paragraphs.title: 2. Make it longer with Extend
paragraphs.text: Suno's help center says Extend lives under Remix and Edit in the song's menu. Extend a clip, then use Get Whole Song to join the parts into one track.

paragraphs.title: 3. Fix parts instead of starting over
paragraphs.text: Suno says v6 can edit one section of a song from a plain language instruction and change a single word or line. The Song Editor can crop and add fades on any plan, but replacing sections needs Pro or Premier.

paragraphs.title: 4. Download only what you will use
paragraphs.text: Each download counts against your monthly limit, and stems come with that song's download. Listen first, then download the version you want to keep.
How to make a song in Udio

paragraphs.title: 1. Prompt or write lyrics
paragraphs.text: Type a description in the prompt field, or open Custom and choose Write Your Lyrics. Udio can write lyrics for you, or you can paste your own.

paragraphs.title: 2. Extend the clip
paragraphs.text: Udio's help center says a song can be extended up to 10 sections, including an intro and an outro. Paid plans also get Sessions, a timeline view for extending and replacing parts.

paragraphs.title: 3. Share the link
paragraphs.text: Because downloads are off, sharing a link is the only way to get a finished Udio song to someone else.
Before you spend credits in Udio, decide whether you will ever need the audio file. If you will, start in Suno, because Udio has not given a date for bringing downloads back.
What each one is bad at

Suno's free plan is now a demo more than a tool: no downloads by default and no commercial rights. Digital Music News reported mixed early reactions from users to v6. Suno also still faces lawsuits from Universal Music and Sony, so its rules could change again.
Udio's biggest weakness is plain: you cannot export anything. Udio's iOS app also lacks remixing, inpainting and uploads, and there is no Android app, according to its help center.

For most people the choice is simple. If the song needs to end up in a video, a podcast or a release, use Suno on a paid plan and read the commercial rules for your plan. If you only want to hear an idea and send a link to a friend, Udio still does that, and its free credits are enough for a few songs a day. Keep in mind that both companies changed their rules after deals with record labels, so check the download and rights pages again before you pay for a year.
